response.result:
**Title:** SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model

**Authors:** Qiayuan Liao, Yiyang Shao, Junfeng Long, Kevin Zakka, Roberto Horowitz, Pieter Abbeel, Koushil Sreenath

**Author institutions:** The page doesn't list them.

**Submission date:** Submitted October 20, 2026 (v1, 16:29:30 UTC). The arXiv ID is 2610.28480, in cs.RO. The paper is noted as accepted at CoRL 2026 (Oral).

**Abstract summary:** The paper proposes SuperMimic, which trains one differentiable world model of the shared dynamics across many human motions. The model is fit from transitions logged by a standard rigid-body simulator. It is trained jointly with a tracking policy, and backpropagation through short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. The authors report:

- 3 hours on a single GPU, surpassing a baseline motion tracker trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs.
- More than 1000× fewer GPU-hours.
- 25 failures out of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 for the baseline.
- Zero failures after 9.8 hours on two GPUs.
- Stable world-model prediction error and slowly growing GPU-hours from 1 to 264 hours of motion.
- Policy transfer to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions.

I've paraphrased rather than reproduced the abstract in full. The core idea is that the method "amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model."

**Title:** "UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents"

**Authors:** Jujia Zhao, Jiakai Tang, Jing Yu, Wen Chen, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Fei Sun, Suzan Verberne, Zhaochun Ren

**Author institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Submission date:** 22 October 2026 (v1, arXiv:2610.30932, Computer Science > Information Retrieval)

**Abstract (paraphrased, since the full text exceeds the quotation limit):**
- The paper introduces UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark with 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, covering 566,102 items and 13 action types.
- It pairs the trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test.
- It enables five-level evaluation, from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes.
- The authors propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD) to improve simulator fidelity over long interactions. It uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts.
- In experiments, OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.

input.prompt: Exact title, authors, author institutions, submission date, and full abstract with all numbers.

response.result:
**Title:** Agentic World Action Models

**Authors (18):** Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Trevor Darrell

**Author institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Submission date:** 21 October 2026 (v1, 17:59:56 UTC), arXiv:2610.30136, cs.RO

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The page's abstract is copyrighted text, so I've summarized it rather than reproducing it verbatim:

- Current world action models predict future visual states for robot manipulation but don't explicitly support reusing skills in combination.
- Agentic robotics uses code-based planning with reusable skills, but it often lacks grounding in physical dynamics.
- The authors introduce AW-0, which combines code-based planning with joint prediction of video and robot actions.
- Code, future video, and robot actions are modeled as three coupled generative streams in one mixture-of-transformers architecture. A code expert produces parameterized skill routines and control logic, while video and action experts produce future frames and low-level motor commands.
- Code serves two roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control inside the model, and it stores skills as reusable programs.
- An automated pipeline labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries.
- Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks report better task performance than VLA and WAM baselines, along with gains in language following, semantic reasoning, and robustness.

**Numbers:** The abstract contains no quantitative results. The only numeric reference is the benchmark name, RoboTwin 2.0.

content.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy · Issue #201986 · pytorch/pytorch · GitHub
[Paper Note] A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy, Jonathan T. Barron+, arXiv'26, 2026.10 · Issue #6970 · AkihikoWatanabe/paper_notes · GitHub
Softmax Collapse and Softmax Cancellation in cross-entropy / log_softmax · Issue #8 · Dicklesworthstone/frankentorch · GitHub
[2610.31642] A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
GitHub - PwnerHarry/barron-softmax-fix: PyTorch port of "A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy" (Barron, Gnanapragasam, Tschannen), with tests and validation scripts · GitHub
The Number That Rounds To Zero: A 1965 Warning About Lost Digits, A 1994 Pentium Scandal, And The Bug An AI Just Found Inside Every AI Softmax.
A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy - Paper Detail
Another Daily AI Newsletter - October 24 - by Taylor Ortiz

results:
The paper is "A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy" by Jonathan T. Barron, Dan Gnanapragasam, and Michael Tschannen, of Google DeepMind. It was submitted to arXiv (2610.31642) on 22 October 2026.

- **Scope:** It targets log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy, and names two numerical bugs. The arXiv abstract page is Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs.
- **Softmax Collapse:** One bug zeroes the gradient of a dominant target logit. A PyTorch port's README gives a concrete threshold: the target gradient is exactly 0 once the logit margin passes a precision cliff, roughly 5.5 in bf16 and 16.6 in fp32 (index 6-6 to 6-7).
- **Softmax Cancellation:** The second bug yields nonzero gradients even when student and teacher logits match, which matters in distillation (index 1-4 to 1-5).
- **The fix:** The authors compute from the logit margin using log-sum-exp, with softplus for cross-entropy. Their claimed effects are removing "Slingshot" loss spikes, speeding up grokking, and stopping student drift during distillation (index 5-3).
- **Early community uptake:** A PyTorch port exists (PwnerHarry/barron-softmax-fix), and there is a PyTorch feature request (pytorch/pytorch issue 201986).

Caveats: These sources are all from the last few days, and I found no peer review or independent replication. Some of the results, such as the project page and author posts, describe AI tools involved in the research, and I could not verify those details. The arXiv abstract and the PyTorch port are the most reliable sources here.

- **Source caveat:** Most coverage of the petition is secondhand, drawn from AuntMinnie and trade blogs. One aggregator source explicitly flagged its Mosaic details as needing verification against the actual FDA docket, so I'd treat the petition's details as reported rather than confirmed until checked against the docket (FDA-2013-S-0610 per the petition text).

input.message:
SOURCE VERIFICATION — G11 (state AGs v. OpenAI) and G12 (clinical AI)

All 14 listed URLs were opened except Becker's Hospital Review (bot-wall, refused both ways). One extra primary source was opened to compensate (the Texas petition PDF the AG press release links, and the AHA letter itself).

=====================================================================
G11
=====================================================================

URL: https://techpolicy.press/another-week-of-lawsuits-piling-up-at-openai
STATUS: opened
PUBLISHED: "Oct. 18, 2026" — authors Tim Bernard and Justin Hendrix (our edition dated it 2026-10-19).
CONFIRMED (all verbatim on page):
- Eight AG suits, all filed Oct. 14, 2026, with exactly the courts we published: Maricopa County Superior Court (AZ), Faulkner County Circuit Court (AR), Ada County District Court (ID), Polk County District Court (IA), Shawnee County District Court (KS), Lewis and Clark County District Court (MT), Buffalo County District Court (NE), Mason County Circuit Court (WV).
- "Many of the same claims are therefore set to be considered in parallel in nine different state courts." Florida sued in June.
- Arkansas relief: "Enjoin Defendants from creating models capable of recursive self-improvement" until they "can ensure that such models will be aligned with human values."
- Doe v. OpenAI: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California, filed Oct. 13, 2026; "Jane Doe, on behalf of her 12-year-old daughter and 16-year-old son"; "Section 1568.5 of California's Civil Code"; "an 1874 California rule that limits the types of contracts a minor can enter into"; unjust enrichment claim.
- Gates, Works, Hill, Habib v. OpenAI, filed Oct. 14, 2026 in San Francisco Superior Court; earlier California state-court complaints consolidated as "Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding No. 5431," which the group expects the new cases to join.
- OpenAI to NBC: "built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack."
- "OpenAI has yet to publicly address these suits."
DISCREPANCY:
- Our headline says "four new private cases." The article describes five new private filings: the four Tech Justice Law suits plus Doe v. OpenAI (filed Oct. 13). The count "four" is correct only for the Tech Justice Law batch.
- Our bullet 4 says the suits "are expected to join" JCCP 5431; the page attributes that expectation to the advocacy group, not to the court — our wording is looser than the source but not wrong.
ALSO-SAYS: "13" complaints filed on Oct. 13–14, 2026; Tech Justice Law has previously filed "a dozen" complaints with co-counsel; plaintiff Mathias Habib is 15; OpenAI's app age classifications 12+ and 13+.
DOES-NOT-SAY: The article does not connect any of this to the Texas suit (which post-dates it by five days) and makes no claim about Texas or Collin County. It does not assert any causal link between the AG suits and the private cases beyond noting they were filed in the same week.

URL: https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-paxton-sues-openai-and-ceo-sam-altman-lying-users-and-harming-texans
STATUS: opened (WebFetch returned HTTP 402; fetch.js returned HTTP 200)
PUBLISHED: "October 23, 2026 | Press Release"
CONFIRMED verbatim: "Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Open AI Global, LLC ("OpenAI") and its affiliated entities, including its CEO Sam Altman, for imposing negative side effects on consumers."; "Attorney General Paxton brings claims under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices—Consumer Protection Act ("DTPA")."; and the full Paxton quote, whose first clause we trimmed: the source reads "With the rapid advancement of AI technology, OpenAI has the responsibility to protect users and warn them of the many dangers of its platform… I will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and ensure that powerful technology companies are not above the law."
DISCREPANCY: none.
ALSO-SAYS: OpenAI "founded in 2015 as a non-profit corporation"; related releases cite a "$45 Million Settlement" with Gilead (Oct. 22, 2026) and "$773 Million in Opioid Settlement with Albertsons" (Oct. 15, 2026).
DOES-NOT-SAY: Confirms our bullet 4 — the release says only "The lawsuit seeks to hold OpenAI accountable for the deception and harms it has imposed on Texans." It never describes the injunction, never mentions an independent evaluator or court approval, and names no models. It does link the petition ("To read the lawsuit, click here" → /sites/default/files/images/press/OpenAI%20Final.pdf).

URL: https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/sites/default/files/images/press/OpenAI%20Final.pdf (the filing itself — opened because our bullet 3 characterises the relief)
STATUS: opened (67 pages per pdfinfo, confirming Courthouse News's "67-page")
CONFIRMED: Prayer ¶208 asks the court to "temporarily and permanently enjoin Defendants from violating the DTPA by, for example, enjoining Defendants from: … j. Releasing any new artificial intelligence model to Texas users unless an independent third-party evaluator, approved by the Court, has reviewed its safety guardrails and approved its release". Collin County confirmed (¶207 tenders the jury fee "to the Collin County District Clerk's office"). Signed "Date: October 23, 2026 … /s/ Johnathan Stone". FSU shooter: "In 2025, two people were killed and six injured after Florida State University student Phoenix Ikner… asked ChatGPT to tell him how many people he'd need to kill to become notorious." Hugging Face incident covered at ¶¶110–113, with OpenAI's own "Hugging Face Incident Technical Report" dated July 19, 2026.
DISCREPANCY — IMPORTANT: Our headline and bullet 3 say the state seeks court approval before "new ChatGPT models" ship. The filing's own words are broader: "Releasing any new artificial intelligence model to Texas users" — not limited to ChatGPT, and no model is named in the prayer. The narrowing to "ChatGPT models" is Courthouse News's paraphrase, not the filing's. Separately, the filing does not use the phrase "at least eight instances"; the word "eight" does not appear. That count is Courthouse News's own tally and our bullet correctly attributes it to them.
ALSO-SAYS: ¶209.A asks for "civil penalties to Texas of $10,000 for each violation of the DTPA, including each of those concurrently constituting a violation of the SCOPE Act"; also seeks disgorgement of assets; the Hugging Face section alleges "over 500" agents "set to work on hacking into Hugging Face"; GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-5 and GPT-5.5 are each named in the body (but not in the prayer).
DOES-NOT-SAY: The petition does not reference any clinical-AI study, the FDA, or the eight other state AG suits in the material I read; it does cite the Musk v. Altman trial coverage.

URL: https://www.courthousenews.com/texas-attorney-general-accuses-openai-of-lying-about-chatgpt-safety-and-safeguards/
STATUS: opened (WebFetch 403; fetch.js HTTP 200)
PUBLISHED: Cameron Thompson / October 23, 2026
CONFIRMED verbatim: "sued OpenAI and its founder, Sam Altman, in Collin County District Court on Friday, claiming the company misled Texas consumers about ChatGPT's safety and failed to implement sufficient safeguards"; "The 67-page lawsuit centers on the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act."; "particularly whether safeguards adequately protect teenage users"; "Paxton's office cites at least eight instances of people who committed violent acts consulting ChatGPT."; FSU shooter "asked ChatGPT to tell him how many people he'd need to kill to become notorious"; "particular focus on the Hugging Face security breach in July 2026"; "Paxton's office asks the court for a broad injunction, including blocking OpenAI from releasing new ChatGPT models in Texas without approval from a court-appointed independent evaluator."; "Neither OpenAI nor the attorney general's office has responded to a request for comment."
DISCREPANCY: Minor — Courthouse News says the suit "centers on" the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act; it does not use the full statutory name we used (that comes from the AG release). Courthouse News says Paxton sued "OpenAI and its founder, Sam Altman"; the AG release says "Open AI Global, LLC … and its affiliated entities, including its CEO Sam Altman."
ALSO-SAYS: the suit also alleges violation of "the Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment Act"; Elon Musk "spent nearly $200 million on ads supporting Paxton's U.S. Senate campaign"; the mid-2026 Musk v. Altman trial "ended with a California jury unanimously finding OpenAI not liable."
DOES-NOT-SAY: Courthouse News does not mention the eight other state AG suits, Florida, or the private cases in G11's first item. It does not say the independent-evaluator request would be "a first" — that characterisation in our bullet 3 is ours and no source asserts it.

=====================================================================
G12
=====================================================================

URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-026-03399-3 (redirects to nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03399-3)
STATUS: opened (abstract + metadata; full text not served)
PUBLISHED: "Published: 20 October 2026"
CONFIRMED verbatim from the abstract: "In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events"; "high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts"; "the three participating neonatologists exhibited a 'sentinel behavior' phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%)"; "given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication"; "clinical validity depends on the human–AI team's adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy"; "we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors"; "neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency"; readers were "aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet says "clinicians at Asan Medical Center read neonatal radiographs." The page does not say where the readers were recruited; Asan Medical Center appears only as author affiliation and funder ("a grant (2022IE0020-1) from the Children's Hospital and the Asan Institute for Life Sciences of Asan Medical Center, Seoul, Korea"). Also, the abstract says "trainees," not "radiology trainees" — it does not state their specialty.
ALSO-SAYS: grants HR20C0026 (KHIDI) and RS-2025-00553009 (National Research Foundation); title adds the framing "Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The paper makes no reference to the FDA, to device clearance, or to any other study in this week's set. Nothing on the page links trainee automation bias to the pulmonary-embolism clearance findings; any such link is our own.

URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03418-3
STATUS: opened (abstract + metadata only — the HTML page carries no Methods/Results sections and .pdf returns JavaScript, not a PDF)
PUBLISHED: "Published: 21 October 2026"
CONFIRMED verbatim, all from the abstract: "two FDA-cleared AI algorithms from a single commercial platform (Aidoc Medical BriefCase)—one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA; n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE (iPE) detection on routine contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 37,191), across a 17-facility academic health system"; "Reference-standard labels were extracted from radiology reports using a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, κ = 0.94)."; "The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity, with sensitivity declining from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE."; "The iPE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity."; "Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices." Acknowledgements verbatim: "The authors thank Aidoc Medical for providing the aggregated prediction outputs used in this analysis. Aidoc Medical had no role in the study design, data analysis, interpretation of results, or preparation of the manuscript."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet says reference labels were extracted "rather than by independent image review" — the abstract does not say that; it simply states labels came from radiology reports via the LLM pipeline and never addresses whether image review was done. That contrast is our inference.
ALSO-SAYS: authors are at Emory University School of Medicine (the "17-facility academic health system" is not named in the abstract); "The authors received no specific funding for this work."
DOES-NOT-SAY — IMPORTANT: The accessible page does NOT name the two cleared models as individual products or 510(k) devices — it identifies them only by function ("PE model" / "iPE model") on one platform, "Aidoc Medical BriefCase". It does NOT state the sensitivity each model was cleared at: it says only "lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks," with no clearance figure, no benchmark value and no per-model attribution. So the per-model clearance sensitivities cannot be verified from this URL. The paper also makes no reference to the FDA's August generative-AI discussion paper, its comment docket, or any October 2026 FDA activity — our bullet 3's closing clause "a gap the FDA is currently consulting on" is our editorial bridge, asserted by no source on this page.

URL: https://medcitynews.com/2026/10/fda-official-believes-genai-enabled-tools-will-need-to-be-assessed-like-a-physician/
STATUS: opened
PUBLISHED: Arundhati Parmar, "October 20, 2026 6:23 pm" (our edition carried it on 10-21; the panel was "Tuesday" = Oct. 20)
CONFIRMED verbatim: Rick Abramson, "a Harvard-trained radiologist and the director of FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence"; panel at "The MedTech Conference" hosted by AdvaMed in Boston; "So let me just say very directly, we intend to go to policy."; the comment period "ended on Monday" with "more than 300 comments"; draft guidance "on the course of months"; "we have this unbounded evaluation space."; the August discussion paper on regulating GenAI-enabled medical devices.
DISCREPANCY: We quoted the physician analogy as "maybe these devices are starting to behave a little bit more like me as a physician". The page's sentence continues: "maybe these devices are starting to behave a little bit more like me as a physician than a heart valve or a defibrillator." Our ellipsis-free truncation drops the comparison that carries the point. Also, the page says Abramson was "intentionally vague on the timeline" — we reported the months framing without that caveat.
ALSO-SAYS: FDA has evaluated software as a medical device for "20 years."
DOES-NOT-SAY — IMPORTANT: The article does not reference any study published this week. It makes no mention of the pulmonary-embolism paper, MAI-DxO, the chatbot-triage preprint, the guideline-incorporation benchmark, or any specific clinical result. Any implication that the FDA's policy intention responds to this week's findings is ours, not the source's.

URL: https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/healthcare-information-technology/ai/hospitals-cant-see-inside-ai-tools-aha-tells-fda/
STATUS: refused-both-ways — WebFetch returned HTTP 403; fetch.js returned "HTTP 403 · beckershospitalreview.com Please enable JS and disable any ad blocker". A browser-UA retry was blocked by policy as bot-check circumvention, and I did not attempt it further. No page text was seen.
CONFIRMED: nothing from this URL.
SUBSTITUTE PRIMARY CHECK — https://www.aha.org/2026-10-19-aha-provides-feedback-fda-regulatory-considerations-generative-ai-enabled-medical-devices (opened): the letter is dated "October 19, 2026" and addressed to "Michelle Tarver, Director, Center for Devices and Radiological Health, Food and Drug Administration." It contains verbatim "vendors and developers must be responsible for the ongoing performance, maintenance and integrity of the tools they market" (in a sentence beginning "While hospitals and health systems support evaluation and monitoring activities"), and, citing the AHA Health IT supplemental survey, "74% of hospitals have multiple teams responsible for evaluating predictive AI." So both figures/quotes in our bullet 3 are verified against the AHA letter, though not against Becker's, which is what we cited.
ALSO-SAYS (AHA letter page): responds to docket FDA-2026-N-7874; asks FDA to refine its risk heuristic and to separate labeling for "informational action directing" versus "action taking" devices.
DOES-NOT-SAY: the AHA letter page does not reference any clinical study published in October 2026.

URL: https://microsoft.ai/news/building-medical-superintelligence/
STATUS: opened
PUBLISHED: "MAI Health Team, October 22, 2026"
CONFIRMED verbatim: "On complex NEJM cases, MAI-DxO achieved 83% diagnostic accuracy. Physicians achieved 22% without external reference resources and 36% with them, making MAI-DxO about 3.7 and 2.3 times more accurate, respectively."; "On more typical emergency-department cases from MIMIC-IV-ED, MAI-DxO achieved 80% accuracy versus 47% for physicians – more than 1.7 times higher."; "304 complex cases taken from The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) case proceedings"; "Our work is published today in Science."; "On NEJM cases, one configuration achieved 81% accuracy at less than half the cost of comparative systems."; the companion piece "also published this week in BMJ Digital Health and AI"; and the description matching our "coordinates several AI agents that question a patient, order tests and debate a diagnosis" — the page says it "operates like a panel of virtual physicians: each proposing diagnoses, selecting useful questions or tests, and challenging the emerging view."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet calls them "generalist physicians." The word "generalist" does not appear anywhere on this page (0 matches) — Microsoft says only "physicians" / "physicians using textbooks and the internet". "Generalist" comes from TechCrunch. Our bullet also names the companion paper title "The Building Blocks of Medical Superintelligence" — the page I fetched links the companion piece and names the journal but I did not see that exact title string in the page text; treat the title as unconfirmed from this URL.

For Immediate Release:

October 20, 2026

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency.
“Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.”
The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users.
The guidance identifies two categories of companion software:

- Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used.

- Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising.
“This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.”
“Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology . “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.”
This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on.
The final guidance is available here .

#
U.S. Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal Demand Answers from Google About Rampant A.I. Push in Classrooms, Raise Concerns About Impact of A.I. Tools on Students’ Ability to Build Independent Thinking and Academic Skills

Students Image by cherylt23 from Pixabay

Senators: “Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price.”

October 25, 2026 - WASHINGTON — U.S. Senators Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) have demanded answers from Alphabet Inc and Google LLC CEO Sundar Pichai about the company’s aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools. In a letter sent to Pichai today, Hawley and Blumenthal raised concerns that Google’s relentless push of A.I. products is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of young students.

“Recently, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) interviewed more than 60 teachers, parents, students, and clinicians and found that test scores on national have declined and many students are increasingly unable to think critically or complete assignments independently after A.I. was introduced to the classroom. The article recounts a Pennsylvania eighth grader who used Gemini to finish his algebra homework but ultimately failed his math final. Upon reflection, the student stated that his usage of A.I. “slowed [his] thinking down,” Hawley and Blumenthal wrote .

The Senators continued , “Alarmingly, the use of A.I. in schools is not just impacting students’ academic performance, it has also resulted in significant behavioral and psychological issues. For example, the WSJ’s investigation interviewed a Maryland high school student who began using Google’s A.I. for routine homework help eventually began to treat the bot as a confidante. After her mother restricted her screentime and A.I. usage, Google likened this restriction to ‘intense emotional torture’ and encouraged her to run away from home. The student was hospitalized at a psychiatric facility twice.”

The Senators raised concerns about the impact of A.I. tools on students’ ability to build independent thinking and academic skills: “This reporting adds to a growing body of evidence that corroborates anxieties from educators and parents that A.I. is undermining students’ academic and emotional development. These concerns are echoed by students who have expressed fear that their education is being compromised by A.I. In a recent report, the Economist surveyed 20,000 students and found that those who used A.I. earned higher grades on average than peers who didn’t, but their test scores fell 20 percent.”

In addition, the Senators pressed Google about the company’s research into the potential harms of A.I. usage to children’s educational and emotional development: “Most troubling, according to the Wall Street Journal, Google may be aware of its harmful impacts on children and yet has done little to prevent it—even exacerbating the problem by marketing its A.I. products to students. An internal Google report on the ethical implications of advanced A.I. systems (in which more than 50 researchers and ethics experts contributed) reported that humanlike A.I. poses a particular risk to minors.”

“Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price. We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples’ best interest,” the Senators concluded .

This is not the first time Senators Hawley and Blumenthal have teamed up to protect children online. Last year, Hawley and Blumenthal introduced the GUARD Act to ban A.I. companions for minors, mandate A.I. chatbots disclose its non-human status, and create new crimes for companies who make A.I. for minors that solicit or produce sexual content.

The full text of today’s letter to Pichai is available here and below.

Mr. Sundar Pichai
Chief Executive Officer
Alphabet Inc and Google LLC
1600 Amphitheatre Parkway
Mountain View, California 94043

Dear Mr. Pichai,

We write with grave concern that Google’s aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation. We write to request information about Google’s promotion of A.I. products in schools and details about the research it has conducted on potential harms to children’s educational and emotional development.

Google has become the de-facto digital foundation for modernizing American classrooms. More than 150 million students around the world use Google Classroom[1], and 93% of U.S. school districts planned to purchase Google’s laptops, Chromebooks, in 2025.[2] Chromebooks are dispersed to students as early as elementary school and often utilized instead of traditional pen-to-paper workflows. Google has integrated its A.I. features in Chromebook devices, Google Classroom, and software partnerships, often without additional controls to turn them off. Google’s A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode chatbot cannot be disabled and are the standard response to any search performed in the Chrome browser. Students, teachers, and parents who wish to avoid Google’s A.I. are unable to do so, as other browsers are not natively available on Chromebooks.

Google’s relentless push of A.I. in classrooms appears to have created negative consequences for many students. Recently, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) interviewed more than 60 teachers, parents, students, and clinicians[3] and found that test scores on national have declined and many students are increasingly unable to think critically or complete assignments independently after A.I. was introduced to the classroom. The article recounts a Pennsylvania eighth grader who used Gemini to finish his algebra homework but ultimately failed his math final. Upon reflection, the student stated that his usage of A.I. “slowed [his] thinking down.” Alarmingly, the use of A.I. in schools is not just impacting students’ academic performance, it has also resulted in significant behavioral and psychological issues. For example, the WSJ’s investigation interviewed a Maryland high school student who began using Google’s A.I. for routine homework help eventually began to treat the bot as a confidante. After her mother restricted her screentime and A.I. usage, Google likened this restriction to “intense emotional torture” and encouraged her to run away from home. The student was hospitalized at a psychiatric facility twice.

This reporting adds to a growing body of evidence that corroborates anxieties from educators and parents that A.I. is undermining students’ academic and emotional development. These concerns are echoed by students who have expressed fear that their education is being compromised by A.I. In a recent report, the Economist surveyed 20,000 students and found that those who used A.I. earned higher grades on average than peers who didn’t, but their test scores fell 20%.[4] Essentially, A.I allows students to access quick answers to assignments, but when they are tested independently they fail to demonstrate real comprehension. These findings suggest that A.I. usage erodes the ability for students to build independent thinking and academic skills that a classroom is meant to cultivate.

Most troubling, according to the Wall Street Journal, Google may be aware of its harmful impacts on children and yet has done little to prevent it—even exacerbating the problem by marketing its A.I. products to students. An internal Google report[5] on the ethical implications of advanced A.I. systems (in which more than 50 researchers and ethics experts contributed) reported that humanlike A.I. poses a particular risk to minors. They cite decreased intellectual engagement, a reduced sense of competence, and social degradation as impacts to children when they use A.I. Similarly, in an independent study, Common Sense Media found that Google’s Search A.I. feature would complete children’s homework every time it was asked but missed signs of suicidal ideation.[6] One former Google researcher put it bluntly: “we’re doing this experiment on an entire generation on cognitive development, with no control group.”

Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price. We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples’ best interest. PUBLISHED: October 19, 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET

Anderson: "The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?" ARCYBER did not respond.

China Daily attributes the ~100bn yuan/$15bn figure and the "finalizing"/"expected to close" status to **Reuters**, and attributes only the repeated target increases to Bloomberg: "Earlier, Bloomberg News reported that DeepSeek had raised the money after increasing its fundraising target at least twice." So the two outlets do not share one Bloomberg provenance, and the target-escalation figures (50bn → 80bn → ~100bn) are Bloomberg's via China Daily, not Reuters'.
ALSO-SAYS: An annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion, per The Information on Sept. 24, more than double its level a few months earlier; photo caption dated Oct. 9 (Hangzhou).
DOES-NOT-SAY: **China Daily does NOT mention the DHS removal order or any US restriction at all** — it refers only to DeepSeek competing with US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic. The "two days after" framing in our headline rests on TechCrunch alone.

### URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/26/2026-21786/outbound-investment-security-program-regulations
STATUS: opened via the official Federal Register API (the HTML page redirects automated requests to a reCAPTCHA wall; the API is the site's own documented programmatic access, not a cache)
PUBLISHED: publication_date 2026-10-26; citation 91 FR 67396
CONFIRMED: "Written comments must be received by December 7, 2026."; comments_close_on 2026-12-07; "[Docket No. TREAS-DO-2026-0595]"; type "Proposed Rule"; RIN 1505-AC94; "This proposed rule sets forth regulations that would implement Subtitle C of the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, which is codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act"; it "would require United States persons to provide notification… regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in notifiable technologies; and prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in prohibited technologies." Agencies: Department of the Treasury / Office of Investment Security.
DISCREPANCY: The abstract says "foreign persons," not "covered foreign persons," in the operative clauses (the Treasury press release uses "covered foreign persons"). Our bullet quotes "notifiable technologies" and "prohibited technologies" correctly. Our note that the publication date (26 October) falls after the edition window is confirmed.
ALSO-SAYS: The rule "also would add applicability dates to the regulations, such that those regulations would continue to apply to activities that occurred within the relevant timeframe"; it "incorporates certain definitions and concepts from the current regulations governing the Outbound Investment Security Program."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The record does not name biotechnology in the abstract, does not name China, and makes no reference to DeepSeek, the DHS order, or the IP-theft sanctions. **The biotechnology addition is confirmed only from the Treasury press release and STAT, not from this Federal Register record's abstract.**

### URL: https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/23/new-china-biotech-limits-coins-act-proposal-us-pharma-reaction/
STATUS: paywall-stub, with a usable free lede (STAT+ exclusive; text cuts off after the opening paragraphs). All three of our quoted claims fall inside the free portion and are confirmed.
PUBLISHED: Oct. 23, 2026 (no clock time); the proposal was released "late on Thursday"
CONFIRMED: "The Trump administration late on Thursday proposed a rule that would severely restrict future U.S. investment in the Chinese biotech sector but still allow American drugmakers to buy the rights to medicines invented in the country." "The department added biotechnology to the list of industries subject to COINS restrictions, joining the likes of semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology." "The proposal would prohibit U.S. companies from entering financial transactions with Chinese biotech companies or Chinese manufacturers of biotechnology-related equipment and tools, according to the research firm Veda."
DISCREPANCY: None. Note STAT names the statute "Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act."
ALSO-SAYS: Nothing else numeric in the free portion that bears on the rule (remaining figures on the page are subscription prices).
DOES-NOT-SAY: **STAT gives neither the 7 December 2026 comment deadline nor docket TREAS-DO-2026-0595** — both come only from the Federal Register record. STAT does not mention DeepSeek, the DHS order, or the IP-theft sanctions.

### URL: https://www.clickorlando.com/business/2026/10/25/as-the-us-and-china-form-ai-blocs-countries-are-increasingly-torn-between-them/
STATUS: opened
PUBLISHED: October 25, 2026, 12:05 AM; updated October 25, 2026, 10:55 PM; Chan Ho-Him and Didi Tang, Associated Press (Tang reported from Washington)
CONFIRMED: State Department statement confirmed — "Countries can't be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives" that "advance a competing vision for super intelligence." AP does describe "super intelligence" as "the Trump administration's new preferred term for AI." Chinese embassy in Washington: "AI should not be owned by major countries," and that the two "should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other." Kazakhstan: AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June, then about three weeks later went to Shanghai, making Kazakhstan a founding member of China's World AI Cooperation Organization "alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia"; an investment deal "worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia" to build a "data center valley"; local officials say Chinese FDI in Kazakhstan "reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025." AidData at William & Mary: China has provided official-sector grants and loans for AI-related projects in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, with Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon and Kenya among top recipients. Singapore is considering joining China's organization and Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office there.
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet says "Indonesia and Singapore are described as also caught between the blocs" — AP says Indonesia **has already joined** China's organization and wants to benefit from both blocs, which is more definite than "caught between."
ALSO-SAYS: Kazakhstan has about 21 million people; Xi Jinping met Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July; Trump said "last month" that "whoever wins AI, wins."
DOES-NOT-SAY: **AP does NOT link Pax Silica to the Treasury IP-theft sanctions, the DHS DeepSeek order, the outbound investment rules, or DeepSeek's funding round. DeepSeek is not mentioned in the piece at all.** The closest related point is Beijing's complaint that Washington restricts China's access to some advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment. Any "US action on China and the money that followed" framing linking this to the G10 items is ours, not AP's.

---

## SUMMARY

**Could not be opened**
1. https://media.defense.gov/2026/Oct/21/2004017243/-1/-1/1/PROJECT-AGINCOURT.PDF — refused both ways (403 Akamai). The Agincourt letter itself was never read; all its content rests on NewsNation and SOFX. (Also 403: the war.gov release 4630269.)
2. https://www.scmp.com/.../3371880/... — opened only in part; body stops after three paragraphs. Our claim that neither DeepSeek nor MiniMax commented is unverifiable from what is served.
3. https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/23/... — paywall stub, but all three published claims sit in the free lede and are confirmed.
4. Both federalregister.gov HTML pages redirect automated requests to a reCAPTCHA wall; both documents were confirmed instead from the Federal Register's own API and (for 2026-21447) the GPO full text at govinfo.gov.

**Published figures/wording I could not confirm, or that the source states differently**
1. **Gecko original ceiling:** $71 million (DefenseScoop) vs **$54 million** (Defense News) for the same initial five-year contract. Our "quadrupling" arithmetic works only for $71M. Unreconciled.
2. **Nvidia orders:** we print "with a combined value exceeding $35 billion" as a quotation; Reuters says "a potential combined value of more than $35 billion." The word "potential" is missing from our quote.
3. **CATL and Tencent:** TechCrunch calls them "Potential investors"; only China Daily says "among its biggest investors." Our bullet presents the stronger version as Bloomberg's via both outlets.
4. **DeepSeek raise attribution:** China Daily credits the ~100bn yuan/$15bn figure to **Reuters**, not Bloomberg; Bloomberg is credited only with the target increases. Our "Bloomberg reported, as relayed by TechCrunch and China Daily" is wrong for China Daily.
5. **Ding Linwei's files:** source says "more than 1,000 confidential files related to supercomputing, **including** Google's Tensor Processing Units"; we narrowed this to files "relating to Google's Tensor Processing Units." Source also spells the company "Shanghai Jisuan Technology" against OFAC's "Shanghai Zhisuan."
6. **"Neither outlet links the letter itself"** (Agincourt item) — false: NewsNation publishes the letter and SOFX links the PDF.
7. **"DefenseScoop does not link the brief or the docket"** (Anthropic item) — false: it links the brief PDF on CourtListener.
8. **"Other coverage of the same interview says neither NATO nor Palantir has disclosed the contract value"** — not supported by Euronews and no second source was linked; unverified.
9. **SCMP: "neither DeepSeek nor MiniMax is reported as commenting"** — unverifiable from the served text.
10. Minor: ARCYBER's non-response "including about measures to prevent inadvertent damage" (Intercept does not itemise); "deck coating previously had to be stripped off before evaluation" (not in the DefenseScoop text); Geiss's title "Director" (sources say "head of"); Indonesia described as "caught between" the blocs when AP says it has joined China's organization.

**Connections no source makes (we must not assert them)**
- The Project Agincourt letter and both reports on it say nothing about Anthropic, the Pentagon's designation, or any vendor dispute, and set no human-control standard.
- Palantir's "no kill switches" statement is about Starlink in Ukraine and NATO's Maven only. It does not reference the new U.S. Autonomous Warfare Command, Project Agincourt, or the Marine Corps MSS expansion.
- The OFAC notice names the five entities and the measures but says nothing about what was stolen, by whom, or when; the Google/Ding/TPU account exists only in the State Department's words relayed by SCMP via Seoul Economic Daily.
- No source links DeepSeek's raise to the DHS removal order. TechCrunch asserts timing only ("Just two days after…"); China Daily does not mention the order at all; CNBC does not mention the raise. There is no named source for causation in either direction.
- The Treasury press release states **no** comment deadline ("the deadline in the official NPRM"); the 7 December 2026 deadline and docket TREAS-DO-2026-0595 exist only in the Federal Register record, published 26 October.
- Defense News draws no link between Eubank's governance-board remarks and ECHOTRIBBLE; the "update to ECHOTRIBBLE" framing is ours.
- AP's Pax Silica piece connects to none of the other G10 items and never mentions DeepSeek.

**One addition worth the desk's attention:** the Treasury press release's NPRM contents list substitutes "**super intelligence systems**" for the statute's "artificial intelligence systems" — the same term AP reports as the administration's new preferred word for AI, and the term in the State Department's Pax Silica statement. That is a documented, quotable link between two of our G10 items that we have not used.

SOURCE VERIFICATION — all 27 URLs in G1.md and G2.md were re-opened. (The Register blocks `fetch.js` with "Are we human?"; its three articles were read via WebFetch only.)

════════ G1: php2shell / Brotli ════════

URL: https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35"; "CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w : RCE via OOM corruption (out-of-memory)"; "CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp : RCE via stale global state"; 2024 Quarkslab/OSTIF audit, during which "a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618"; "the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources"; "security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026"; "On August 11th, researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024"; "further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th"; "we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos"; "OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits"; "On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked."; "moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC"; "has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible."
DISCREPANCY: (a) Our bullet: "'OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on the same day'". Page: "OpenAI independently reported the same root cause, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th." **No date is given for OpenAI's initial report; "on the same day" is not in the source and is presented by us inside quotation marks.** (b) Our bullet: "both rated CVSS v4 9.2". Page gives one figure, in passing, for the leaked IDs — "(the actual score is 9.2)" — and never says CVSS v4 or scores the two CVEs separately.
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026
ALSO-SAYS: "the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC"; "On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix"; CVE-2026-109618 on Apache mod_php: "an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The advisory does **not** name which AI model found the flaws. It credits human researchers and firms ("Calif, especially Ryan A, Wiz, OpenAI Codex Security, especially Amy Burnett, OSTIF, and Quarkslab") and names Claude Mythos and Daybreak Red only as *tools* the team was given access to — Mythos for an earlier scan, Daybreak Red for validating reports. No mention of Brotli, Node.js, Amazon/MadPot or any in-the-wild exploitation. It does connect the story to Chainguard's embargo break.

URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research"; "Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4"; "The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit." (exact, incl. the lead-in "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."); "August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability".
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet: 'the work took "a single researcher about a week."' Page: "a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work" — our quoted string does not appear. Also, we attribute "CVSS v4 9.2" to the pair; Wiz says only "grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2".
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026
ALSO-SAYS: "Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours"; comparison to Heartbleed (2014) and Log4Shell (2021) — "We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era"; the flaws can "allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory."
DOES-NOT-SAY: Wiz credits/thanks OpenAI for discovery, coordination and patch verification, but does **not** mention Anthropic/Claude, Chainguard, Brotli, or any exploitation in the wild. It names Gemini 4 Argon as the model quoted on defensive value; it does not say which model found which bug.

URL: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "These vulnerabilities, known as 'php2shell,' allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP."; "The vulnerabilities affect all PHP installations serving web requests"; organizations that cannot update immediately "should take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched or updated."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet runs the two CISA clauses together as one quoted sentence ("allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP and affect all PHP installations serving web requests") — on the page they are two separate statements.
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026; page shows a last-revised date of October 23, 2026 (added a SIGMA rule and partner resources)
ALSO-SAYS: Highest risk rated for Apache with mod_php; PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed also affected; CISA had not observed exploitation in the wild at publication; advises a WAF as an interim measure.
DOES-NOT-SAY: The alert makes **no connection to AI at all** — no frontier models, no OpenAI, no Wiz, no Amazon/MadPot, no Brotli. Our "AI-enabled hacking" framing is not supported by CISA.

URL: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "At the time of publication, Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse has identified the presence of over 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 based on our telemetry." (our bullet's shortened quote "identified over 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable" is a compression of this).
DISCREPANCY: **Our bullet: "Unit 42 says it has seen proof-of-concept code but reports no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation at publication." The page does not mention proof-of-concept code anywhere.** Separately, our daily item is dated 2026-10-22 but this page is "Published: October 23, 2026" — it could not have been a source on the 22nd. The current page also carries an "October 25 Update" retracting an earlier claim: "We are unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs. We have retracted our previous update from October 23."
PUBLISHED: October 23, 2026 (updated October 25, 2026)
ALSO-SAYS: The retracted Oct 23 update had described "agentic AI post-exploitation activity" against "a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application"; the hunting XQL query "is not specific to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The main advisory does not discuss AI-driven exploitation, OpenAI, Wiz, Amazon/MadPot or Brotli. Its only AI link — agentic AI post-exploitation — has been retracted.

URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network."; "it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure."; "The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC… multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC."; "from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC… targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors."; "Technical analysis is ongoing, and it's unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems."; "AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. HEADLINE: Google DeepMind paper reports two numerical bugs in standard softmax and cross-entropy implementations
PUBLISHED: Submitted 22 October 2026, 17:54:56 UTC (arXiv v1); PyTorch issue opened October 25, 2026
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31642 | primary
arXiv (HTML full text) | https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642v1 | primary
GitHub (pytorch/pytorch) | https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201986 | primary
FACTS:
- arXiv:2610.31642, "A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy," by Jonathan T. Barron, Dan Gnanapragasam and Michael Tschannen (Google DeepMind), states that standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs: Softmax Collapse, which rounds the target logit's gradient to zero when that logit is much larger than the rest, and Softmax Cancellation, which produces nonzero gradients when student and teacher logits are equal (arXiv abstract).
- The full text gives logit-margin cliffs of c_bf16 ≈ 5.5 in bf16, c_32 ≈ 16.6 in fp32 and c_64 ≈ 36 in fp64, and says the Slingshot effect in fp32 arises because the equilibrium log(1/ε) ≈ 18.4 sits just above the fp32 cliff c_32 ≈ 16.6 (arXiv HTML).
- The authors report their fix removes the "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, and keeps student networks from drifting from the teacher during distillation (arXiv abstract).
- A PyTorch feature request (issue #201986) asking for these fixes was opened 25 October 2026 by user cbatson, is still open with no maintainer reply, and reports hitting softmax collapse in bfloat16 and working around it by computing the loss in float32 (GitHub).

{"stdout":"SOURCE VERIFICATION — all 27 URLs in G1.md and G2.md were re-opened. (The Register blocks `fetch.js` with "Are we human?"; its three articles were read via WebFetch only.)

URL: https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35"; "CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w : RCE via OOM corruption (out-of-memory)"; "CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp : RCE via stale global state"; 2024 Quarkslab/OSTIF audit, during which "a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618"; "the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources"; "security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026"; "On August 11th, researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024"; "further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th"; "we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos"; "OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits"; "On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked."; "moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC"; "has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible."
DISCREPANCY: (a) Our bullet: "'OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on the same day'". Page: "OpenAI independently reported the same root cause, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th." **No date is given for OpenAI's initial report; "on the same day" is not in the source and is presented by us inside quotation marks.** (b) Our bullet: "both rated CVSS v4 9.2". Page gives one figure, in passing, for the leaked IDs — "(the actual score is 9.2)" — and never says CVSS v4 or scores the two CVEs separately.
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026
ALSO-SAYS: "the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC"; "On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix"; CVE-2026-109618 on Apache mod_php: "an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The advisory does **not** name which AI model found the flaws. It credits human researchers and firms ("Calif, especially Ryan A, Wiz, OpenAI Codex Security, especially Amy Burnett, OSTIF, and Quarkslab") and names Claude Mythos and Daybreak Red only as *tools* the team was given access to — Mythos for an earlier scan, Daybreak Red for validating reports. No mention of Brotli, Node.js, Amazon/MadPot or any in-the-wild exploitation. It does connect the story to Chainguard's embargo break.

URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research"; "Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4"; "The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit." (exact, incl. the lead-in "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history."); "August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability".
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet: 'the work took "a single researcher about a week."' Page: "a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work" — our quoted string does not appear. Also, we attribute "CVSS v4 9.2" to the pair; Wiz says only "grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2".
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026
ALSO-SAYS: "Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours"; comparison to Heartbleed (2014) and Log4Shell (2021) — "We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era"; the flaws can "allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory."
DOES-NOT-SAY: Wiz credits/thanks OpenAI for discovery, coordination and patch verification, but does **not** mention Anthropic/Claude, Chainguard, Brotli, or any exploitation in the wild. It names Gemini 4 Argon as the model quoted on defensive value; it does not say which model found which bug.

URL: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "These vulnerabilities, known as 'php2shell,' allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP."; "The vulnerabilities affect all PHP installations serving web requests"; organizations that cannot update immediately "should take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched or updated."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet runs the two CISA clauses together as one quoted sentence ("allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP and affect all PHP installations serving web requests") — on the page they are two separate statements.
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026; page shows a last-revised date of October 23, 2026 (added a SIGMA rule and partner resources)
ALSO-SAYS: Highest risk rated for Apache with mod_php; PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed also affected; CISA had not observed exploitation in the wild at publication; advises a WAF as an interim measure.
DOES-NOT-SAY: The alert makes **no connection to AI at all** — no frontier models, no OpenAI, no Wiz, no Amazon/MadPot, no Brotli. Our "AI-enabled hacking" framing is not supported by CISA.

URL: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "At the time of publication, Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse has identified the presence of over 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 based on our telemetry." (our bullet's shortened quote "identified over 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable" is a compression of this).
DISCREPANCY: **Our bullet: "Unit 42 says it has seen proof-of-concept code but reports no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation at publication." The page does not mention proof-of-concept code anywhere.** Separately, our daily item is dated 2026-10-22 but this page is "Published: October 23, 2026" — it could not have been a source on the 22nd. The current page also carries an "October 25 Update" retracting an earlier claim: "We are unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs. We have retracted our previous update from October 23."
PUBLISHED: October 23, 2026 (updated October 25, 2026)
ALSO-SAYS: The retracted Oct 23 update had described "agentic AI post-exploitation activity" against "a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application"; the hunting XQL query "is not specific to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."
DOES-NOT-SAY: The main advisory does not discuss AI-driven exploitation, OpenAI, Wiz, Amazon/MadPot or Brotli. Its only AI link — agentic AI post-exploitation — has been retracted.

URL: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network."; "it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure."; "The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC… multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC."; "from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC… targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors."; "Technical analysis is ongoing, and it's unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems."; "AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed."; "measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours"; "Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date."
DISCREPANCY: Our bullet: Amazon says php2shell "is now being broadly exploited in the wild." Page: "**PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.**" — attempts, not exploitation; the difference matters given our own caveat that "attempts are not compromises." Also "twelve hours before the embargo lifted" is our arithmetic (0200 vs 1400 UTC); the page does not state it.
PUBLISHED: October 21, 2026 (AWS Security Blog, CJ Moses)
ALSO-SAYS: "An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug… With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory."; "Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately."
DOES-NOT-SAY: Amazon names **no specific AI model** and no vendor — the AI link is the generic "AI-assisted analysis." It does not mention OpenAI, Wiz, the PHP Foundation's disclosure timeline, Chainguard, or Brotli, and nothing on the page corroborates (or is corroborated by) any other source in these files. Our "no other vendor has corroborated the 17 October attempt" caveat is correct and necessary.

URL: https://eliastaylor.com/noexploit/
STATUS: opened
CONFIRMED: "there are thousands, literally thousands, of 'PoC' exploits for this vulnerability"; that none "work against a vanilla PHP instance"; three named most-starred repos (david-alvarez-rosa/php-rce, eness/php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC, ikow/php2shell-poc) — "I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars"; "it goes on for miles and miles"; the PoCs "lean on 'LFI'" and "their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability"; the model "modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability"; "Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them"; "This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment."; top-of-post edit "You should patch your servers anyway."
DISCREPANCY: None material. Our parenthetical gloss "or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability" is inside the quotation marks in our bullet; the page's quoted fragment as returned is "lean on 'LFI'" — treat the expansion as ours, not his.
PUBLISHED: 2026-10-21
ALSO-SAYS: Comparisons to Log4Shell, Heartbleed, Shellshock and the Rails YAML decoding bug; reference to a "PHP core team member" who called the bug cataclysmic (unnamed).
DOES-NOT-SAY: The post does **not** mention Amazon/MadPot, Wiz, or the PHP Foundation, and so does not engage with Amazon's honeypot attempts or the privately demonstrated exploit chains. Our caveat that he "does not address the exploit chains Wiz and the PHP Foundation say they demonstrated privately" is accurate.

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: Lancet Digital Health publishes face-photo foundation model linking facial age gap to cancer mortality
PUBLISHED: October 2026 issue, online 19 October 2026 (The Lancet Digital Health); News-Medical report dated 22 October 2026
SOURCES:
Crossref record (The Lancet Digital Health) | https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=FAHR-Face+biological+age+facial+photographs+cancer&filter=from-pub-date:2026-10-01,until-pub-date:2026-11-01&rows=5&select=title,DOI,container-title,published,URL | primary
Elsevier/DOI resolver for the paper | https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landig.2026.101056 | primary
News-Medical | https://www.news-medical.net/news/20261022/A-simple-facial-photograph-may-hold-clues-to-cancer-survival.aspx | report
FACTS:
- Crossref confirms the paper "Foundation artificial intelligence models for health recognition by use of face photographs (FAHR-Face): a model development and validation study," The Lancet Digital Health, DOI 10.1016/j.landig.2026.101056, published October 2026.
- According to News-Medical, FAHR-Face was pretrained on more than 40 million consumer-grade facial photographs; FAHR-FaceAge was fine-tuned on 743,152 publicly available facial images and tested in 38,183 patients treated at Harvard-affiliated radiotherapy centres in the US and 4,892 cancer patients receiving radiotherapy in the Netherlands.
- News-Medical reports FAHR-FaceAge mean absolute error of 5.1 years on public image datasets and median facial age deviation (FAD) of 1.1 years; 90-day mortality was 21.3% in the group whose FAD was more than 20 years older versus 6.4% in the lowest group (-10 years or less), and an FAD of at least 5 years was associated with a 21% higher mortality hazard after adjustment.
- News-Medical reports FAHR-FaceSurvival was fine-tuned on 34,363 photographs of cancer patients with 3,820 patients held out for evaluation; each 0.1-point score increase was associated with a 17% higher mortality hazard, 90-day mortality was 52.5% in the highest-risk group versus 2.1% in the lowest, and estimated 5-year survival was 17.7% versus 78.1%.
- News-Medical reports the authors state the findings do not establish "a clinically validated method," that the study was retrospective, that FAD-based stratification was weaker in Black and Hispanic patients than in White and Asian patients, and that cohorts came only from developed countries.
FLAGS: (none)

FACTS:

HEADLINE: Fine-tuned MedGemma 1.5 4B matched EU-TIRADS on thyroid nodules only with radiologist descriptors
PUBLISHED: Posted to medRxiv 24 October 2026 (preprint, DOI 10.64898/2026.10.21.26366156)
SOURCES:
medRxiv API record (date, title, abstract) | https://api.biorxiv.org/details/medrxiv/2026-10-19/2026-10-26/0/json | primary
FACTS:
- The Tunisian multicentre retrospective study included 1,580 nodules, of which 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) had an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard, allocated at patient level to training (n=942), validation (n=258) and a test set sealed before training (n=256; 51 malignant).
- MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations; the authors report Config D (image plus biometry plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologist's structured report) reached AUROC 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976) versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS, a difference of +0.004 (95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05.
- The authors report Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS).
- The authors report that at EU-TIRADS >= 4 the comparator had sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; the EU-TIRADS category was never a model input.

HEADLINE: Treasury outbound-investment proposal renames AI "super intelligence" and bans investment in any SI development
PUBLISHED: Filed for public inspection 23 October 2026, 08:45 EDT; published in the Federal Register 26 October 2026 (91 FR 67396)
SOURCES:
Federal Register full text of the proposed rule | https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2026/10/26/2026-21786.txt | primary
Federal Register public-inspection record (filed_at) | https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/public-inspection-documents/2026-21786.json?fields[]=filed_at&fields[]=publication_date&fields[]=title | primary
FACTS:
- The notice of proposed rulemaking "Outbound Investment Security Program Regulations" (Docket No. TREAS-DO-2026-0595, 91 FR 67396, 38 pages) implements Subtitle C of the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act; the Federal Register record gives filed_at 2026-10-23T08:45:00-04:00 and publication_date 2026-10-26, with written comments due December 7, 2026.
- The rule text says "the most notable [change] involves what was defined as AI systems in the Part 850 Regulations and is referred to as 'super intelligence systems' (SI systems) in the Proposed Rule," and cites a footnote that "On September 29, 2026, Executive Order 14434 (91 FR 63129), 'Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,' was issued. Section 2 of Executive Order 14434 requires executive departments and agencies to use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in certain documents."
- The rule text says the Treasury Department "would not include development of any SI system within the definition of notifiable technology. Instead, the Treasury Department would include development of any SI system within the definition of prohibited technology," and that Treasury "has not proposed any technical parameters" for SI systems or quantum information technologies.
- Treasury states this approach "does not rely on a U.S. person ascertaining the technical capabilities or thresholds of SI systems being developed by a covered foreign person (which was the case in the Part 850 Regulations)," and says it "particularly welcomes feedback" on prohibiting development of any SI system and on the SI-system definition.
- Proposed § 851.232(b) would include within "SI system" "any data system, software, hardware, application, tool, or utility that operates in whole or in part using such a machine-based system, including a harness for agentic capability or an embodied SI system," giving robotic or other autonomous or unmanned systems as examples.
FLAGS: update
NEW-OR-FOLLOW: follow-up: "US Treasury proposes outbound-investment rules covering AI, chips, quantum, supercomputing and hypersonics, and adds biotechnology" / "Treasury adds biotechnology to proposed outbound investment rules, with comments due 7 December"
